title: All beings
hookLine: east, west, north, south, above, below; seen and unseen

lines: A CITY AT NIGHT FROM A PLANE.
cards: A plane at night, and below you the lights of a city. Every little light is a kitchen, a hallway, somebody's night shift. Thousands of lives you'll never meet, all at once, too many to hold one by one.
Today, metta stops going person by person. For a week you've practiced with one face at a time. Now the old texts open the window all the way.
Every direction. Every being. All of them.

teach.b: In several Pali discourses, two of them cited today, the same description of the practice appears almost word for word.
A person dwells, the text says, with a mind full of loving-kindness, spreading it toward one direction, then the second, the third, the fourth.
Then above, below, and all around, everywhere, to the whole world, with a mind that's vast, grown great, without measure, without hostility.
East, west, north, south, above, below: a map of the whole world drawn from where you sit. And this step has no faces. You don't have to picture everyone; you couldn't.
You let the wish travel outward, like light, with no edge. The Visuddhimagga, the old manual, gives lists to help: may all beings be well, all breathing things, all creatures, all persons.

teach.h: SEEN AND UNSEEN, BORN AND UNBORN.
teach.b: The Metta Sutta, which you'll meet tomorrow, adds more: the weak and the strong, the long and the short, the seen and the unseen, those living near and far away, those born and those still to be born.
That last pair means the wish reaches people who don't exist yet.
The Buddhist word for this is appamaññā, the immeasurable. Metta is one of four immeasurables, called that because it has no boundary. Not your family.
Not your country. Not your species.
Everywhere. Of course the mind drifts back to one or two faces. That's fine.
Let them be two lights among all the others.

how: A metta session often ends by extending the wish to all beings in every direction, as the Pali texts describe, often using lists like all beings, all breathing things and all creatures.

o: every human being on this planet

games.q: what the texts reach for — tap the pairs.
p: the whole world from where you sit
reaching people who don't exist yet

s: this stage needs you to picture every face
it has no faces: you let the wish travel outward, like light.
the Metta Sutta wishes well to beings not yet born
it names those born and those still to be born.
metta is called immeasurable because it has no boundary
it's one of the four immeasurables, reaching everywhere.

games.q: you're sending metta in every direction, and your mind keeps going back to one face. what do you do?
o: let that face be one light among all the others.
games.why: drifting is normal. the face becomes one light among many, and the wish keeps going outward.

practice: After a moment of metta for yourself, send the wish out one direction at a time, taking your time with each: in front of you, behind you, to your left and right, above, the sky and whatever's in it, and below, the floors under you and the whole earth: may all beings there be well.
Finally let it go everywhere at once, like a light with no lampshade.

wordCard.voice: All beings. Metta sent in every direction, above, below and all around, without measure.

orig.note: Pali: the immeasurables, the four boundless states, of which metta is the first.

carryVoice: Your line: everywhere. Above, below and all around, with no edge at all. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: DN 13, Tevijja Sutta; MN 7, Vatthupama Sutta: the pervasion of the directions
